neurips-2020-bridging-imagination-and-re.tldr: BIRD links imagined and real trajectories to improve model-based reinforcement learning.
paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning can save real interactions by planning through trajectories generated by a learned world model. But an overfit world model can make those imagined experiences misleading, trapping policy improvement in a poor local solution. This paper targets the mismatch between simulated planning and actual environment behavior.

The proposed algorithm, BrIdging Reality and Dream, or BIRD, maximizes mutual information between imaginary and real trajectories. Its intended effect is to make improvements learned through imagination transfer more readily to trajectories encountered in the real environment.

Experiments on challenging visual-control benchmarks show improved sample efficiency and state-of-the-art performance in the reported comparisons. The abstract does not supply scores or identify the benchmarks, and it does not guarantee that the learned model becomes accurate everywhere. The contribution is an explicit training connection between imagined and real experience, supported by control-task evaluations.

neurips-2020-convbert-improving-bert-wit.tldr: ConvBERT combines local dynamic convolutions with global attention to reduce language-model training cost.
paragraphs: BERT’s global self-attention is expensive, yet some attention heads mainly learn local dependencies. This paper treats that behavior as computational redundancy and proposes replacing those heads with span-based dynamic convolutions that directly model local context.

The remaining self-attention heads and new convolutional heads form a mixed attention block. ConvBERT incorporates this block into a BERT-style model, combining mechanisms for global and local information rather than making every head inspect the full sequence in the same way.

Evaluations across downstream tasks report stronger performance than BERT and its variants with fewer parameters and lower training cost. ConvBERTbase achieves a GLUE score of 86.4, 0.7 above ELECTRAbase, using less than one-quarter of its training cost. These figures describe the stated model comparison; the abstract does not provide a general cost bound or per-task results for every language-understanding application.

neurips-2020-de-anonymizing-text-by-fing.tldr: Input-dependent nucleus-sampling behavior can expose text through implementation side channels.
paragraphs: The paper examines a privacy risk in the implementation of machine-learning text generation. Nucleus sampling changes the set of eligible next tokens depending on the preceding text. The authors ask whether those input-dependent operations can reveal information even when the text itself is not directly exposed.

Their main finding is that the sequence of nucleus sizes forms a unique fingerprint for many natural English word sequences. They show how an attacker could infer typed text by observing such fingerprints through a suitable side channel, with cache-access timing given as an example.

The paper discusses how this could help link anonymous text to a user and considers defenses. The abstract does not claim that every deployment exposes the necessary side channel or that every possible sentence has a unique fingerprint. Its contribution is identifying an implementation-level leakage mechanism and showing why generation procedures deserve security scrutiny alongside their model outputs.

neurips-2020-expandnets-linear-over-para.tldr: ExpandNets train compact networks through temporary linear expansion that can be algebraically removed.
paragraphs: Overparameterization can make neural networks easier to optimize, but a deployed model may need to remain compact. This paper proposes training a larger parameterization of the desired compact network while preserving the ability to recover the original network form at inference.

Each linear layer is expanded into multiple consecutive linear layers without inserting nonlinearities. Because the composition remains linear, it can be contracted algebraically after training. The authors introduce two convolutional expansion strategies and evaluate them in image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation.

Experiments outperform both direct training of the compact network and knowledge distillation from a teacher. Additional observations show reduced gradient confusion during training and improved generalization. The abstract gives no numerical gains or training-cost comparison. The distinctive result is that training can benefit from extra parameters while inference uses the contracted compact architecture.

neurips-2020-generative-causal-explanati.tldr: A generative model learns latent factors whose changes influence a classifier’s output.
paragraphs: Post-hoc explanations should clarify which changes in an input affect a classifier’s decision. This paper learns a low-dimensional generative representation whose latent factors influence the output statistics of a trained classifier. The stated causal meaning concerns interventions on these learned factors and their effect on the classifier.

The training objective balances faithful modeling of the data distribution with information-theoretic measures of causal influence on predictions. It produces both global and local explanations without requiring labeled attributes or a known causal structure. The classifier must provide class probabilities and a gradient.

Controlled test cases illustrate how the objective behaves, followed by image-recognition demonstrations. The abstract does not report numerical explanation-quality scores. Its causal claim should remain tied to changes within the learned generative representation; it does not by itself establish the real-world causal relationships that originally produced the observed data.

neurips-2020-hynet-learning-local-descri.tldr: HyNet improves local visual descriptors through normalization-aware similarity and training design.
paragraphs: Local image descriptors support tasks such as matching image patches and reconstructing three-dimensional scenes. This paper studies how L2 normalization changes the gradients used to train those descriptors, then uses the resulting observations to design a new descriptor called HyNet.

HyNet combines a hybrid similarity measure in a triplet-margin loss, a regularization term that constrains descriptor norms, and an architecture that applies L2 normalization to intermediate feature maps as well as final descriptors. The changes jointly address the training signal and the representation produced by the network.

Experiments report substantial improvements over prior methods on patch matching, verification, and retrieval benchmarks. HyNet also outperforms complete end-to-end alternatives on three-dimensional reconstruction tasks. The abstract does not give benchmark scores or isolate the contribution of each component, so the evidence supports the combined descriptor design in those evaluations rather than a quantified benefit from normalization alone.

neurips-2020-learning-from-failure-de-bi.tldr: A deliberately biased model identifies examples that help a second model resist spurious correlations.
paragraphs: Classifiers often exploit a dataset’s easy but unreliable correlations instead of learning the intended task. This paper observes that such reliance is especially pronounced early in training when the spurious pattern is easier to learn. It uses that behavior to construct a debiasing signal.

Two networks train together. The first is deliberately encouraged to amplify its bias, while the second focuses on examples that contradict the first network’s predictions or prejudice. The method uses a cheaper, more generic form of human knowledge than explicitly labeling every spuriously correlated attribute.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show substantial improvements across several bias types, occasionally exceeding methods that use explicit attribute supervision. The abstract does not specify that generic knowledge or provide numerical gains. The result concerns resistance to evaluated spurious correlations, rather than a guarantee that the resulting classifier satisfies every social or statistical notion of fairness.

neurips-2020-learning-linear-programs-fr.tldr: A differentiable optimization framework learns linear-program costs and constraints from observed optimal decisions.
paragraphs: Linear programs are usually specified through known costs and constraints. In inverse settings, only examples of optimal decisions may be available, and the optimization problem itself must be inferred. This creates a challenging bilevel learning problem because model parameters affect the solutions used to compute the training loss.

The authors propose a gradient-based framework that jointly learns all parameters with flexible cost, constraint, and loss parameterizations. They address issues specific to linear programs, including empty feasible regions and multiple optimal decisions. A batched PyTorch implementation of a homogeneous interior-point algorithm supports implicit differentiation or backpropagation.

Experiments successfully learn synthetic linear programs and minimum-cost multicommodity-flow instances outside the direct scope of previous methods. The abstract does not claim unique identification of the original program from every dataset. Its contribution is a flexible computational framework for learning optimization models, supported by these demonstrations.

neurips-2020-least-squares-regression-wi.tldr: Markov-dependent regression has stricter limits, while experience replay helps on structured processes.
paragraphs: This paper studies least-squares regression when observations come from a Markov chain rather than independent sampling. It establishes sharp minimax lower bounds involving the chain’s mixing time under different noise settings, showing that dependence can make the problem fundamentally harder.

In the worst case, a simple method called SGD-DD, which uses roughly one observation per mixing time, is minimax optimal. Constant-step-size SGD can be strictly worse despite its optimality for independent-data regression. Even for Gaussian autoregressive dynamics, ordinary constant-step-size SGD does no better than SGD-DD.

The authors then introduce an experience-replay-based algorithm with a significantly better error rate for that structured setting. This supplies theoretical support for replay beyond the worst-case subsampling baseline. The improved rate is specific to the analyzed process structure and does not contradict the general minimax lower bound over all relevant Markov chains.

neurips-2020-myersonian-regression-039e2.tldr: Myersonian regression formalizes pricing-sensitive linear prediction and gives approximation and hardness results.
paragraphs: Pricing errors are asymmetric: a price above a buyer’s value can lose the entire opportunity, while a lower price leaves some revenue uncollected. Motivated by online-advertising pricing, this paper studies linear regression with a discontinuous loss reflecting that distinction.

For an example with value v, the loss is v if the prediction exceeds v, and otherwise v minus the prediction. The authors prove exact optimization is NP-hard and, assuming the Exponential Time Hypothesis, rule out a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme.

They nevertheless obtain a polynomial-time approximation scheme with additive error epsilon times the number of examples in revenue. Its dependence on inverse accuracy is exponential in a polynomial, while its dependence on input size is polynomial. The algorithm is also shown to be stable and to generalize over sample distributions. These results characterize an accuracy-computation tradeoff, rather than promising efficient exact optimization.

neurips-2020-retrieval-augmented-generat.tldr: RAG combines a sequence generator with retrieved Wikipedia passages for knowledge-intensive language tasks.
paragraphs: Language models store knowledge in their parameters, but retrieving precise facts, updating them, and exposing provenance remain difficult. This paper combines a pretrained sequence-to-sequence model with external nonparametric memory to support language generation grounded in retrieved material.

The external memory is a dense vector index of Wikipedia accessed by a pretrained neural retriever. The authors compare one formulation that uses the same retrieved passages throughout an output sequence with another that can use different passages for different generated tokens.

Fine-tuning and evaluation cover multiple knowledge-intensive tasks. RAG sets state-of-the-art results on three open-domain question-answering tasks, beating parametric sequence models and task-specific retrieve-and-extract systems. For generation, outputs are more specific, diverse, and factual than a strong parametric-only baseline. The abstract supports comparative improvements, not a guarantee that retrieved passages or generated answers are always correct.

neurips-2020-safe-reinforcement-learning.tldr: An automatic instructor learns when to activate reset controllers during reinforcement learning.
paragraphs: An agent in a safety-critical environment must avoid costly mistakes while it is still learning. This paper proposes an instructor-based alternative to exploration methods that depend on particular smoothness assumptions and probabilistic safety priors.

A monitor has a library of reset controllers and activates them when the agent begins behaving dangerously. It need not know how to solve the task or possess a model of the environment. Because different interventions affect learning progress differently, a teacher learns a policy for selecting reset controllers, creating a curriculum aimed at improving final policy reward.

Experiments in two environments demonstrate curricula for safe and efficient learning. The abstract does not give numerical results or describe how reset-controller reliability is established. The safety mechanism depends on that intervention library and monitoring setup; it is not evidence that an arbitrary unmonitored agent can explore real-world environments safely.

neurips-2020-trajectory-wise-multiple-ch.tldr: Specialized dynamics heads and context adaptation improve model-based control under changing dynamics.
paragraphs: A dynamics model trained for one environment may fail when the transition behavior changes. This paper treats that variation as multimodal and introduces trajectory-wise multiple choice learning, a model-based reinforcement-learning method with several prediction heads.

Training updates the head that predicts a trajectory most accurately, encouraging different heads to specialize in environments with similar dynamics. A learned context vector summarizes dynamics-specific information from past experience, allowing online adaptation to unseen environments. During planning, the system selects the head that best predicts recent experience.

Evaluations across multiple control tasks show stronger zero-shot generalization than state-of-the-art reinforcement-learning comparisons. The abstract does not supply task names or numerical gains. Its contribution is the combination of dynamics specialization, contextual adaptation, and adaptive planning; the reported generalization does not imply accurate prediction under every possible change in environment dynamics.

neurips-2020-woodfisher-efficient-second.tldr: WoodFisher uses an efficient inverse-Hessian estimate to guide neural-network pruning.
paragraphs: Curvature information can reveal how changing a network’s parameters affects its loss, making it useful for compression. But existing approximations may be inaccurate or expensive. This paper examines their quality and introduces WoodFisher as a faithful, efficient estimate of the inverse Hessian.

The compression method builds on the Optimal Brain Damage and Optimal Brain Surgeon framework. It uses the curvature approximation to guide pruning, and the authors also extend the approach to incorporate first-order information. Additional capabilities include choosing layer-specific pruning thresholds and operating with limited data.

WoodFisher substantially outperforms popular alternatives for one-shot pruning. It also improves test accuracy over state-of-the-art approaches when iterative gradual pruning is allowed, including on ImageNet ILSVRC. The abstract does not give sparsity levels or exact accuracy gains, so the comparative findings should be understood within the evaluated compression configurations rather than as an unconditional pruning guarantee.

neurips-2021-a-realistic-approach-to-gen.tldr: Realistic synthetic masks expand face datasets and improve recognition on masked-face benchmarks.
paragraphs: Face-recognition datasets collected before widespread mask wearing contain few masked faces. This paper augments existing images by placing synthetic masks onto faces using SparkAR Studio, with nine mask variants differing in color, shape, and fabric.

The method creates 445,446 masked samples, corresponding to 90% of CASIA-WebFace, and 196,254 samples, corresponding to 96.8% of CelebA. Volunteers compare the generated examples with competing approaches and judge the proposed overlays significantly more realistic.

FaceNet, VGG-face, and ArcFace models trained on the enhanced datasets perform better on masked-face test benchmarks than corresponding models trained on the original unmasked datasets or competing synthetic-mask datasets. The abstract does not provide recognition rates or demographic analyses. The contribution is a data-generation technique and released augmented data, with both perceptual realism assessments and downstream recognition evidence in the tested setting.

neurips-2021-absolute-neighbour-differen.tldr: A neighbor-difference statistic detects dependence expressed through changing variability.
paragraphs: Two variables can be related even when the main signal is a change in variability rather than a simple predictive function. This paper proposes the absolute-neighbor-difference-based neighbor correlation coefficient to detect such nonfunctional associations through heteroscedasticity in unpredictable variation.

The measure can be used alone as a heteroscedasticity test or combined with other statistics to separate functional from nonfunctional relationships. Its construction avoids explicitly estimating regression residuals or a dependence model, which the authors present as reducing reliance on a particular model form.

The mechanisms of the test are established theoretically and illustrated with numerical analyses. The abstract does not state power, calibration, or sample-size results for particular distributions. The supported contribution is a concise statistic designed for an often-overlooked type of dependence, rather than a claim that one correlation coefficient completely describes every possible relationship between variables.

neurips-2021-adaptive-wavelet-distillati.tldr: Adaptive wavelet distillation converts neural-network information into concise multiscale models.
paragraphs: High predictive accuracy can come with models that are costly and difficult to interpret. This paper proposes adaptive wavelet distillation, or AWD, to extract information from a trained neural network into a wavelet transform with an interpretable multiscale structure.

AWD learns the transform by penalizing the network’s feature attributions in the wavelet domain. The resulting model is intended to remain predictive while becoming concise and computationally efficient. The authors develop applications in collaboration with domain experts rather than assessing interpretability solely through a generic visualization.

The demonstrations involve cosmological-parameter inference and molecular-partner prediction. In both settings, the distilled models outperform state-of-the-art neural networks and identify features judged scientifically meaningful in the respective domains. The abstract does not quantify the gains or establish that every network can be distilled equally well. Its evidence supports this approach in the two studied scientific applications.

neurips-2021-asynchronous-stochastic-opt.tldr: An asynchronous optimizer’s convergence depends on average gradient delay rather than the worst delay.
paragraphs: In distributed optimization, workers can return gradients computed from old parameter values. Delays may vary widely because of changing computation and communication loads. This paper studies stochastic optimization with arbitrary gradient delays and seeks guarantees that are not dominated by one unusually slow update.

For smooth nonconvex objectives, the authors give an algorithm requiring O(sigma²/epsilon⁴ + tau/epsilon²) steps to find an epsilon-stationary point, where sigma² is gradient variance and tau is average delay. Earlier comparable guarantees depended on the maximum delay instead.

Experiments show effectiveness and robustness when delay distributions are skewed or heavy-tailed, settings in which the mean can be much smaller than the maximum. The theoretical target is stationarity, not global optimality. The abstract provides no numerical speedups, but the improved delay dependence directly addresses heterogeneous distributed systems where a few slow workers should not dictate the entire bound.

neurips-2021-conservative-data-sharing-f.tldr: Conservative data sharing routes offline experience selectively to improve multitask reinforcement learning.
paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning can draw on data collected for many tasks, but pooling all experience indiscriminately may hurt learning. This paper’s empirical analysis finds that sharing can worsen the mismatch between a learned policy and the available dataset, leading to divergence and poor performance.

The proposed conservative data sharing method, CDS, routes data according to the improvement it provides over task-specific data. It can be combined with multiple single-task offline reinforcement-learning algorithms, making selective sharing a reusable component rather than requiring one entirely new learner.

Tests cover multitask locomotion, navigation, and vision-based robotic manipulation. CDS achieves the best or comparable performance relative to previous offline multitask methods and data-sharing approaches. The abstract does not specify numerical gains or a universal criterion guaranteeing beneficial transfer. Its main finding is that deciding which experience to share matters as much as accumulating a larger offline dataset.

neurips-2021-controlling-neural-networks.tldr: DeepCTRL lets users adjust learned rule strength during inference without retraining.
paragraphs: Rules can encode useful constraints or domain knowledge, but a fixed training objective leaves little flexibility afterward. DeepCTRL incorporates a rule encoder and rule-based objective into a neural network so that rule influence can be adjusted when the trained model is used.

The method creates a shared representation for decision-making and supports rules defined over inputs and outputs. At inference, a user chooses an operating point between predictive accuracy and the fraction of outputs that verify the rule, without retraining the network.

Demonstrations in physics, retail, and healthcare show increased rule-verification ratios and accuracy gains on downstream tasks. The authors also explore rule hypothesis testing and unsupervised adaptation through shared rules. The abstract does not claim every rule is valid or every prediction satisfies it; controllable rule strength exposes a tradeoff whose usefulness depends on the selected rules and application.

neurips-2021-csaw-m-an-ordinal-classific.tldr: CSAW-M directly annotates mammographic masking and supports prediction of clinically important cancer outcomes.
paragraphs: Breast tissue can obscure a tumor in a screening mammogram, a phenomenon called masking. Existing approaches often use breast density as a proxy for this difficulty. This paper introduces CSAW-M to measure masking potential directly rather than relying only on density.

The public dataset contains mammograms from over 10,000 individuals, with masking-potential assessments from five specialists. The authors train deep models to estimate masking levels from these annotations, framing the task as ordinal classification.

The estimated masking is significantly more predictive of participants later diagnosed with interval or large invasive cancers than corresponding breast-density estimates, even though the models are not explicitly trained for those outcomes. The abstract does not provide predictive metrics or clinical deployment evidence. The contribution is an annotated benchmark and evidence that directly modeling masking captures useful information beyond the chosen density-based comparisons.

neurips-2021-diverse-message-passing-for.tldr: Diverse Message Passing gives different node attributes different propagation weights on each edge.
paragraphs: Many graph neural networks propagate all attributes along an edge using the same weight. This paper argues that individual attributes can have different patterns of similarity across connected nodes, so a single node-level notion of homophily or heterophily can hide important variation.

The authors define attribute homophily by treating attributes as weak labels and introduce Diverse Message Passing, or DMP, with attribute-specific edge weights. Two additional strategies reduce computation and help avoid overfitting. Spectral analysis connects existing spectral graph networks to restricted versions of this framework.

Theoretical analysis addresses representational ability and mitigation of oversmoothing. Experiments on real networks report better handling of heterophily and reduced oversmoothing than existing state-of-the-art methods. The abstract does not identify the networks or quantify gains, so it supports the framework’s advantages in those evaluations without establishing that fully attribute-specific propagation is always preferable.

neurips-2021-intermediate-layers-matter-.tldr: Matching intermediate features improves momentum-contrastive pretraining, especially with few medical-image labels.
paragraphs: Momentum contrastive learning aligns representations of differently augmented versions of an image. This paper extends that training signal to intermediate network layers, asking whether useful features can be encouraged earlier in the network rather than only through the usual contrastive objective.

The added loss either minimizes mean-squared differences between intermediate representations or moves their cross-correlation matrix toward the identity. Evaluation covers NIH Chest X-rays, breast-cancer histopathology, and diabetic retinopathy. Both alternatives match or improve standard MoCo, with an average gain of 5% across the three datasets in a 1%-labeled-data setting.

Feature-similarity analysis and layer-wise probing indicate more feature reuse and earlier informative representations. Comparisons of output distributions after fine-tuning with few versus many labels show lower Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance. These analyses support improved pretraining representations in the tested medical-imaging tasks; the abstract does not claim equivalent gains for all datasets or label budgets.

neurips-2021-luna-linear-unified-nested-.tldr: Luna approximates attention by packing and unpacking a fixed-length intermediate sequence.
paragraphs: Standard Transformer attention has quadratic time and memory costs in sequence length, limiting long-context modeling. Luna replaces this computation with two nested linear attention functions that approximate softmax attention while keeping time and space complexity linear.

The first function packs the input into a fixed-length sequence, and the second unpacks that representation. An additional fixed-length input and corresponding output carry contextual information through the nested operation. This intermediate sequence is the mechanism that avoids directly retaining the usual full quadratic interaction structure.

The authors evaluate long-context modeling, machine translation, and masked-language-model pretraining. Results are competitive with or better than strong baselines, including full-rank attention and other efficient sparse and dense methods. The abstract gives no task scores or runtime measurements. Its evidence supports the approximation’s practical effectiveness in these benchmarks without asserting exact equivalence to standard softmax attention.

neurips-2021-m-fac-efficient-matrix-free.tldr: M-FAC computes inverse-Hessian vector products without explicitly storing the full curvature matrix.
paragraphs: Second-order information can improve neural-network optimization and pruning, but its storage and computation can be prohibitive. M-FAC studies matrix-free inverse-Hessian vector products when the Hessian is approximated by a sum of rank-one matrices, as in an empirical-Fisher approximation.

For compression with dimension d and m fixed rank-one terms, the first algorithm uses O(dm²) precomputation, O(dm) per vector product, and O(m) to query an individual inverse-matrix element. A second algorithm handles a sliding optimization window, with O(dm + m²) per product and O(dm + m³) to add or remove a gradient.

Experiments show competitive pruning and optimization results with substantially lower overhead than existing second-order methods. These costs apply to the specified approximation and data structures, not an arbitrary exact Hessian. The abstract does not give numerical accuracy or runtime comparisons, but clearly separates the compression and online-optimization use cases.
